preview: An off-campus interview experience for a Google summer internship, featuring an online challenge and two technical DSA rounds.
content: Interview Experience Google (Off-Campus) Hrim Gandhi, B.Tech CE, 2018-22 Part 1: Google’s Online Challenge: The online test took place on 16th August 2020 and the window was accessible from 3 pm to 5 pm. The test duration was 60 minutes consisting of two coding questions. The proctor of the online test was quite strict, any pop-up or tab switching led to direct termination of the test without any prior intimation for the same. (Of course, you can’t Google in Google's test xD) The questions had partial scoring for test cases. One of the questions was based on string manipulation and the other was based on bit-based dynamic programming. Similar Coding Questions: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/google-internship-2020-google-online-challenge1st-coding-round/?ref=rp https://discuss.codechef.com/t/googles-online-challenge-coding-intern-questions-approach-help/74840 Part 2: Technical Interview There were 2 technical interviews for 45 minutes each. My interviews were scheduled on the 20th and 21st of October at 9:30 pm and 10:30 pm, respectively. The reason for conducting interviews during these non-working hours was that the interviewers were from Mountain View, California, and Sydney, Australia. The interviews were purely based on Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA). This was clearly informed beforehand. Round 1: To my surprise, there were no tell-me-about-yourself questions asked at the beginning of the round. My interviewer just asked me if I had joined the shared Google Doc where the problem statement read as follows: A cat is in a maze, the maze is represented by one N by M matrix (N rows and M columns), which contains: G // Empty ground, the cat could step on or jump over this cell S // Stone, the cat can’t step on or jump over this cell C // Initial position of the cat E // Final position of the cat (Exit) The cat needs to go to the exit. The cat can walk up/down/left/right by 1 step or jump 2 steps (in the same direction) within the maze. One example maze: (N=4, M=3) GCS GSG EGG GGG The minimum answer is 2 minutes. First, go left, then jump down. The given question did not provide all the information needed to solve it. It is quite normal to encounter such a scenario in an interview. The interviewer tests your understanding quotient of the given problem statement and expects the interviewee to ask questions in order to unravel the underlying details and corner cases. For example, I asked why the unit for the final answer was ‘minutes’. He answered that both a step and a jump require the same amount of time, i.e. 1 minute. Then I asked if it was guaranteed that a solution always exists. After getting a clearer idea of the problem statement, discuss a brute force solution so that you can ensure that you have understood the question. Discuss aspects such as time and space complexity along with each solution you provide. Optimize your solution as much as possible. Think out loud. I provided a solution using Breadth First Search (BFS). After I explained my approach I was asked to code the same on the shared Google Doc. It is recommended to practice writing code without an IDE so that you don't face any problems with the time constraint. Clean code and appropriate naming of functions and variables is something that I would personally recommend. Follow up question: What if the cat could jump at most J times? We discussed a few approaches in the remaining 5-10 minutes of the interview. Round 2: Since the interview is only 45 minutes, generally only one coding question is asked of higher difficulty level or two coding questions of easy-medium level. I was asked two questions in this round. The problem statements were: Question 1: When I joined the shared Google Doc the problem statement read as - ‘Introvert cell’. She explained the problem as follows - There is an introverted child who wants to sit on a bench. Since he was an introvert, he preferred to sit as far as possible from any other child. As we can see, she intentionally left out vital details such as input and output. Similar to the previous round, I asked questions to gather more information regarding the problem statement. After discussing the details, the problem statement then looked as follows - Given a binary array (consisting of only 0’s and 1’s), where 0 represented a vacant seat and 1 represented an occupied seat, the task was to find the index of any vacant seat for the introverted child such that the chosen indexed seat is as far as possible from the occupied seats. Provide time and space complexities of your solution at the end. Question 2: Similar binary trees Given two binary trees, answer whether they are similar or not. Two trees are called similar if one of them can be obtained from the other by a series of flips, i.e. by swapping left and right children of a number of nodes. Any number of nodes at any level can have their children swapped. Two empty trees are similar. For example, the following two trees are similar with the following sub-trees flipped: 2 and 3, NULL and 6, 7 and 8. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/tree-isomorphism-problem/ Results There were no HR rounds or any other interviews conducted after the 2 technical rounds. After about a month, on the 14th of November, the eve of Diwali, I received an email from my recruiter offering me a summer internship at Google as an SWE (Software Engineer). Preparation I had used interviewbit.com (one question from each bucket) and geeksforgeeks.com articles for DSA preparation for my campus interviews. After I got the dates for my Google's technical interview, I almost had a month's time to prepare. I started with leetcode.com and did the most common interview questions. It has three categories: easy, medium, and hard from which I completed 35%, 61%, and 41%, respectively. Maximum priority should be given to the medium section as questions are most likely to be of that level of difficulty. I tried reading company-specific archives as much as possible from geeksforgeeks.com and glassdoor.co.in about interview experiences. I also practiced some interview questions that were asked during the campus drives of top tier colleges. All the Best! For any doubts regarding interview preparation, you can contact me at hrimgandhi@gmail.com P.S. It’s okay to be nervous. It’s okay to not stay calm. But don’t let it affect your interview. Be confident about yourself, and everything shall go well.
